session_name: Eastern Corn Belt Plains reference assessment

notes: EPT (mayfly/stonefly/caddisfly) taxa richness; more sensitive taxa indicate better condition.
Benthic Shannon diversity; higher diversity indicates better condition.
Percent tolerant individuals; a higher share of pollution-tolerant taxa indicates worse condition.
Total benthic taxa richness; higher is better.
Chlorophyll a; higher indicates algal enrichment/eutrophication (worse).
Specific conductance; higher indicates ionic disturbance (worse).
Dissolved nitrogen; higher indicates nutrient enrichment (worse).
pH degrades condition at BOTH extremes. Two-sided (optimum) curve: scored 1.0 across the reference interquartile core, falling in both tails.
Total phosphorus; higher indicates nutrient enrichment (worse).
Turbidity; higher indicates more suspended sediment (worse).
Native fish taxa richness; higher is better.
Bankfull width-to-depth ratio; both over-widened (very high) and incised (very low) degrade condition. Two-sided curve centered on the reference core.
Log relative bed stability; higher (nearer natural) is better. Was degenerate in the pilot (Q25 issue), so expect a review flag.
Log mean substrate diameter; coarser substrate generally better, but valley-type dependent.
Large woody debris volume per 100 m; higher is better.
Percent fast-water (riffle/run) habitat; more generally better for many biota. Ecoregion-dependent.
Percent sand and fines; higher indicates fine-sediment loading (worse).
Residual pool depth per 100 m; deeper residual pools generally better habitat.
Channel sinuosity; higher generally indicates a more natural planform.
Mean bankfull height; both incision (very high banks) and over-widening (very low) depart from reference. Two-sided curve centered on the reference core.
Mid-channel canopy density; higher shading generally better for thermal/light regime.
Riparian canopy plus mid-layer plus ground cover; higher is better.
Percent embeddedness; higher means interstitial spaces filled with fines (worse).
Natural fish cover; higher is better.
Base-flow index (% of streamflow from baseflow); a higher baseflow share indicates a more stable, groundwater-supported flow regime.
Dam density (dams per sq km); impoundment alters the natural flow regime and fragments the network.
Watershed cultivated crops (%); row-crop conversion degrades infiltration, soil structure, and runoff timing.
Watershed herbaceous wetland (%); wetlands store surface water and attenuate flow peaks.
Watershed impervious surface (%); imperviousness drives flashier runoff, reduced infiltration, and degraded catchment hydrology.
Watershed woody wetland (%); wetlands store surface water and attenuate flow peaks.
Road/stream crossing density; crossings fragment aquatic habitat and impede organism passage.

Watershed road density; roads concentrate and route runoff to the channel, so higher density means more concentrated inflow pressure. Directional proxy shared with the EASI screening metric; it does not count outfalls.
Mean watershed elevation; physiographic scaling context. Predictor only.
Mean annual precipitation (1981-2010 normal); scaling/climate context, not a condition indicator. Predictor only.
Mean annual runoff; scaling/climate context, not a condition indicator. Predictor only.
